_readme: Deep-dive dossiers written by /book-deep, one JSON object per line after this header, keyed like book-estimates.jsonl. Each holds the per-axis evidence a deep estimate was derived from, so /book-log can re-price it when a rule moves instead of falling back to a screening guess.
_pre: the estimate's est, leanedOn and risks before the dive - kept so a dive can be scored against the real result.
_axes: dep id -> {v, note, src}. v: earns (adds points) | clear (checked, costs nothing) | costs (graded deduction) | fires (hard filter fails, estimate blocked) | unknown (sources do not settle it, so it is a risk).
_actual: set by /book-log when the book is read: the real score. The line stays after the estimate is retired, because a dossier with an actual is the calibration record for dives.

axis:opening.note: Small, 1-3 points; the filter does not fire. The excerpt opens on one concrete scene ('After I shot Vikram we put our things in the car and drove to the airstrip') with Vikram, Miguel and the seed case unexplained, but after about 1,050 words it states the premise outright ('Time travel. More specifically: past-directed time travel... from Kogalym in 2080 to that aircraft in 2028') and flashes back in one linear first-person thread, so neither shape applies. The cost is the out-of-order structure that follows: readers call it 'confusing' at first and say it began 'too cryptically', and two Czech readers say the Triton typesetting leaves timeline switches unmarked ('Nekdy ani stridani casovych linek nebo mluvci v dialogu nebyli oddeleni').

axis:occult.note: Power is conferred by technology and mathematics only: nanospores introduced during an MRI let a pilot's mind ride a host through entangled 'Luba pairs', built on the mother's mathematics of paradox. No rite, invocation or devotion in the mechanism or in its origin.

axis:detective.note: No investigation plot. There is a suspicion strand about who is sabotaging the team and turning members against Valentina ('a great deal of tension and suspicion as to whom is doing this'), resolved as a thriller reveal rather than worked out from clues; a flag, not a deduction.

axis:worldbuilding.note: The declared model is precise (one block-time lattice, paradox as 'noise' that superposes so that 'to an observer that condition always occurred', mind-only travel limited by that noise) and most reviewers say it holds: Locus calls it 'one of the few time-travel stories where I don't feel that the existence of paradox has cheated me', another reviewer says the closing twist 'was 100% predicted and explained and demonstrated earlier in the book; no Deus ex machina', and a Czech reader calls it 'skutecne promysleny'. A minority disagrees: a 2-star Goodreads review says the rules are broken 'at the end of the book just to fit one's narrative', and The Wry Writer (page now offline, quoted from search snippets) calls the ending 'ludicrous' because destroying the experiment should undo Antti's trip; by inference that objection assumes the grandfather paradox the declared superposition rule replaces, so it is priced into the floor rather than held open as a risk.

axis:protagonist.note: Valentina, a 71-year-old teacher of the last generation, is the most praised element ('an interesting character, a woman old enough to remember when the human species had a future'); she must persuade her host rather than command her, carries an estrangement from her mother, and finally puts herself in danger to save the world. Rootable and interesting; the flat-character complaints target the cast rather than her.

axis:motives.note: The Valentina-Tatiana conversations are the book's moral engine: Valentina has to justify the takeover to the woman she occupies, which lets Reynolds 'consider the morality of what Permafrost are doing', and the 2028 strand 'addresses consent'. A Czech reader praises 'motivaci a vnitrnich boju' and characters who question each other's decisions; the thinly motivated side turns are priced under character-differentiation, not here.

axis:ideas.note: Nameable in a sentence: time as a frozen lattice where paradox is noise that settles into one history, travelled only by a mind riding a host who can talk back, with the question whether saving one future builds a worse one. Reviewers who read the trope widely call it new (Locus 'novel'; 'never come across one with THIS particular analogy'; Grimdark Magazine 'fresh'), and a Czech reader: 'Skvele napady... donuti cloveka premyslet'.

axis:short-idea-driven.note: 176 Czech pages; the short form earns nothing by itself, and the idea it carries is real, so it costs nothing either. The suspension can cover the thin side cast but not the lead, who is rootable; the recurring complaint is that it is too short ('Chtel jsem vic'), the opposite of padding.

axis:momentum.note: 'Thriller like pacing... a strong page-turning feel' (Reactor), 'grabs you on page one' (Little Red Reviewer), 'Never should it lag, and this one doesn't' (Elitist), 'Paradni jizda od zacatku az na konec' (databazeknih). The dissent is about getting in, not drive: one reader 'took several tries', another says it 'starts slowly'.

axis:character-differentiation.note: Small, 1-3 points. The central pair are sharply contrasted ('a real contrast between Valentina and Tatiana'), but the rest is thin: 'Vsechny postavy pusobili plose' and Cho and Miguel change behaviour without any hint (databazeknih), 'the story and characters become rather forgettable' (Pyles of Books), and a 3-star Goodreads review says the sabotage story behind the resolution comes only in 'hints and short, secondhand discussions'.

axis:bleakness.note: Small, 0-2 points. 2080 is the last generation, with starvation and 'mobile euthanisation clinics', a mercy killing and a pilot trapped in an animal host; 'very little funny going on... Actually nothing at all'. Relieved by a rescue mission and an ending reviewers call 'wistful, and melancholy but hopeful' and 'bittersweet': the self-sacrifice shape, not unrelieved grimness.

axis:life-phase.note: A 71-year-old lead. The axis has only ever cost for a child's inner life and older leads pay nothing; her interiority in the excerpt is adult and purposeful (fear for her pupils, grief over Vikram).

axis:multi-pov.note: One first-person narrator throughout ('Valentina remains our storyteller throughout, though her body is not always her own'); the complexity is chronology, not viewpoints.

axis:density.note: No padding: under 180 pages, and the complaint runs the other way ('criminally short', 'Chtel jsem vic').

axis:unearned-competence.note: Valentina walks with a cane after a stroke and cannot fly the plane; being the first to time-embed is explained by her civilian-medical implants and by a deeper link to the project that the book reveals.

axis:prophecy.note: No prophecy. Foreknowledge is technological and declared limited ('The noise swamps us long before we ever get close to doing anything really stupid'), so it is judged under worldbuilding.

axis:sex-portrayal.note: Competence is mixed: the time theory is Valentina's mother's, but Director Cho, a physicist, built the project and designed its control protocol, and Antti is the capable pilot. No one-sided contrast.

axis:sexual-content.note: Content notes: 'Sex: Nope'. The plot is a seed-retrieval mission.

axis:sexual-treatment.note: Nothing to treat: 'Sex: Nope', with 'maybe a handful of strong language'.

axis:infidelity.note: The premise is time travel to save seed stock; no affair appears in any summary, Cho is described as 'very happily' married until his wife's illness, and content notes list no sex.

axis:same-sex-romance.note: No romance of any kind is reported. The pronoun switch one Reactor commenter noticed ('one of the characters just changes sexes... from he to she') is the host mechanic: hosts need not be the same sex or even the same species.

axis:sequels.note: 'A stand-alone novella'; nothing to read first.

readingOrder: volume 1 of Shattered Sea (More strepu); its own arc closes, readable alone

axis:opening.note: Read in the author's sample. One scene in Mother Gundring's chambers: a lesson that defines minister, Gettland and the Tall Gods as it goes, Yarvi's hand and his wish to escape kingship stated, then 'My king' and he knows his father and brother are dead. Complaints are of a flat or whiny first fifth, never of confusion ('od druhe stranky se jde na vec').

axis:momentum.note: Close to unanimous across 125 databazeknih comments (82%, 508 ratings): 'cte se samo', read in under 24 hours, 'chytl v podstate od prvni strany'. Fantasy Hive: 'sailed through it in less than 24 hours'. Dissent puts a flat stretch in the first fifth (Elitist: 'underwhelmed by the first 20-25%'; Fantasy Hive: 'first 50 pages or so just felt a little flat'), not later.

axis:protagonist.note: The sample gives him flaws to overcome on every page (self-pity, cowardice, rage, the hand) and constant self-ironic interiority. Elitist calls the arc 'one of Abercrombie's best', and readers report warming to him. Real complaints: passive in the first third (Izzy46: 'veci se mu jenom deji'; Dear Author: 'very little agency'), and by the end a hard schemer who poisons his mentor ('fakt husty intrikan'). He travels from victim to avenger, not into villainy, so this earns, though not at full weight.

axis:motives.note: The plot runs on a sworn vengeance oath and on motives revealed late. Odem thinks a one-handed king ruins Gettland; Gundring and the High King move against Laithlin's money for 'the greater good', which is the title of chapter one. A modest earn: most page time is rowing, trekking and fights ('dej osekany na prekotne se valici dejovou linku'), and readers ask for more inner life in the cast.

axis:ideas.note: The thinking comes in maxims (strong men are many, wise men few; the lesser evil and the greater good), not a question the characters work through. Czech readers call these 'rado by moudre hlasky' meant seriously and miss depth 'at jsou to postavy, pribeh nebo myslenky'. It does connect, since the chapter-one lesson becomes the logic of the betrayal and of the last scene. Priced a few points under a book that leaves something to think about.

axis:occult.note: There is no magic ('V pribehu se vubec neobjevuje magie'; elf ruins are a dead civilisation that sickens anyone who enters), the invented pantheon never acts, and the sample says ministers faked miracles from passages in the Godshall. But in chapter 4 rites of that invented faith are staged on the page: a prayer-weaver's betrothal blessing, and a ship-funeral where 'Two dozen horses were led onto the ship, and slaughtered so their blood washed the deck' so that Death would receive the dead. The source test passes and the depiction test, read literally, would veto. Because the rite works nothing and this boundary is unruled, the standing guard grades it at a few points; tell the reader before proposing.

axis:detective.note: There is no investigation strand. Odem's betrayal is enacted in front of Yarvi at Amwend, and the Gundring conspiracy is revealed in the last chapter, not investigated.

axis:worldbuilding.note: A sketched Norse facade that readers find credible ('svet uveritelny', 'funkcne minimalisticka svetotvorba'), and the final poisoning is planted in chapter one (black-tongue root 'boiled in water it can't be seen or tasted', the evening tea). The cost: Uthil, the long-lost uncle, happens to be chained on the same galley and keeps saving Yarvi ('obrovska nahoda ... pohadkova'; helpers appear 'nahodile (a prihodne)'). Add doves trained to speak messages, and it comes to a couple of points.

axis:life-phase.note: Yarvi is about sixteen, and the first third reads teen from the inside: self-pity, shame before his mother, frequent tears ('na chlapa az moc casto plakal'; 'zacatek byl uknourany'; Goodreads group: 'too whiny so far'). He hardens through the book, so this is a couple of points, the Ender's Game 87 cost.

axis:childrens.note: Several databazeknih readers cite the author's afterword in the Czech edition saying he aimed at ages 12-16, and the book is simpler than adult fantasy. It is also violent and dark: Common Sense lists a skull split by an axe, and Grimdark Magazine says 'not a children's story'. A YA register cost The Hunger Games 89 nothing; the simplicity is priced under ideas.

axis:multi-pov.note: One close-third viewpoint and one plot line throughout ('Jedna dejova linka'; 'er forma z Jarviho pohledu').

axis:character-differentiation.note: Mixed evidence that nets to neither earning nor costing. Some readers find the oarsmen distinct ('kazdy je jiny, ale dobre se doplnuji'; Elitist 'colorful'); others find them clichéd or flat ('achingly cliched ... Especially Nothing'; 'postavy ploche').

axis:density.note: 328 pages in Czech with no digressions ('bez zbytecnych odbocek'). Most complaints run the other way, that it is rushed, and padding is what this axis prices.

axis:bleakness.note: Slavery at the oar and a frozen trek, held up by friendship among the outcasts. Fantasy Hive: 'the novel lacks any real sense of futility'.

axis:faith.note: Religion is an invented pantheon in the background. The book is wry about its clergy (a pompous prayer-weaver, miracles staged by ministers), and the late reveal makes conversion to the southern One God the conspirators' political tool, but belief itself is never mocked and no real religion is touched. The One God thread grows in the sequels, not here.

axis:prophecy.note: There is no prophecy or chosen-one element. What binds Yarvi is his own sworn oath of vengeance.

axis:unearned-competence.note: He never learns to fight. He wins with the herb lore and cunning of the minister training shown in chapter one, and the swordwork belongs to Nothing, revealed as the legendary warrior Uthil. One reviewer finds the turn from 'whiny teenager' to king too quick.

axis:sexual-content.note: Common Sense rates sex 'very little': one brief light kiss with Isriun and an unspoken attraction to Sumael. Elitist: 'some hand holding, that's about it'.

axis:sexual-treatment.note: There is nothing to be crude about. Czech readers note 'absenci sexuality a platonicke touzeni hlavniho hrdiny' and say 'drsny sex nahradily nevinne pohledy ci doteky'.

axis:infidelity.note: No marriage or engagement is betrayed. Laithlin marries Uthil only after Uthrik's death, which renews their old betrothal.

axis:same-sex-romance.note: There is no same-sex relationship. The only romantic threads are the betrothal to Isriun and Yarvi's attraction to Sumael.

axis:sex-portrayal.note: Clever women (Laithlin, Gundring, Sumael) are matched by clever men (Yarvi, Odem, Grom-gil-Gorm). The Ministry's female lean has an in-world reason ('She Who Writes entrusted woman with the gift of letters'), and Dear Author finds the women 'somewhere in between fully realized and stereotypical', with no men diminished to make a point.

axis:opening.note: The excerpt (reports 1 to 3) opens on one situation with its context in the first paragraph: Charlie is 32, works at Donner's bakery, writes because Dr Strauss told him to, and wants the operation: 'I want to be smart.' One thread and no invented terms, so neither shape of the filter applies. The misspelling (reproduced in the Czech translation) is friction rather than confusion and is priced under momentum.

axis:occult.note: Intelligence is conferred by brain surgery and enzyme injections tested first on a mouse: a laboratory procedure with no rite anywhere in the system. The only charm on the page is Charlie's rabbit's foot, a superstition of the man, not a practice the book stages.

axis:detective.note: No investigation-shaped strand. His late research into Algernon's decline is laboratory science ending in a paper (the Algernon-Gordon Effect), and finding his family is a homecoming, not a puzzle.

axis:worldbuilding.note: One capability is declared and its obligations stay with one man, and the book obeys its own rule: Algernon's decline is shown before Charlie's and the reversal follows a law Charlie derives, so the ending is set up, not sprung ('od počátku bylo jasné, jak se bude vyvíjet a jak dopadne' is that consistency seen from the other side). Minor plausibility dissent only: one Czech reader found the timescale of the change unrealistic, another the IQ testing silly.

axis:protagonist.note: Interesting and rootable with a real flaw: the genius turns arrogant ('as soon as he begins to develop his mental faculties, he becomes insufferable', from a 4/5 review; 'Chytrý Charlie mi byl strašně nesympatický', a 3-star Czech reader), and the direction of travel is back toward warmth as he reconciles with Norma, ends it with Alice and chooses Warren rather than be pitied. His own past is the open question the novel adds: repressed memories of Rose, Matt and Norma surface one by one.

axis:motives.note: The diary puts nearly every page inside one mind: why he wants to be smart (traced in report 13 to his mother's shame), why he cannot touch Alice, what he fears as Algernon fails. Side characters get motives too (Rose's fear, guilt and shame, Norma's resentment). Czech praise centres on exactly this: 'nejlepší románová sonda do psychiky', 'Díky deníkovým zápiskům mu doslova vidíte do hlavy'.

axis:ideas.note: Several nameable ideas, sustained to the end: intelligence without emotional growth isolates; a disabled man treated as a lab animal by the people who 'made' him; whether he was happier before. Readers say it left them thinking ('Být chytrý není totéž co být moudrý'), and the one 3-star reader who could not name the lesson is describing a question left open, not a missing one.

axis:sexual-content.note: Not the plot: remove the sex and the experiment, the rise and the fall all remain. Filter 6 does not fire.

axis:sexual-treatment.note: A recurring thread, not a chapter: his mother's fury at a boyhood erection, panics with Alice, a park pickup ending in a false rape accusation, an affair with neighbour Fay used to cure his anxiety, a lyrical night with Alice, and in decline pornographic magazines and watching a woman bathe across the courtyard. Explicitness is low ('no explicitly sexual scenes', 'they aren't detailed') and the handling is Freudian psychology, not the crude kind behind Ready Player One 55, but the volume is well past the one chapter that drew the single complaint on Válka starého muže 87 (a Czech reader: 'Hodně mě štvali ty milostné pletky a místama a líčení kolem sexu'). Volume is unmeasured, so priced at roughly 3 to 8 points with the range widened.

axis:infidelity.note: Charlie, Alice and Fay are all unmarried and unengaged, so the Alice/Fay overlap is outside the axis's scope. The one marriage is a stranger in a single park scene who recounts her own infidelities as backstory; nothing is shown or approved.

axis:same-sex-romance.note: None. The only touch is Fay asking whether he is homosexual after a drunken night; he says he is not.

axis:bleakness.note: Sad, with loneliness as a theme (genius as isolation) and child abuse recalled; several low-rating Czech readers call it depressing ('docela depresivní příběh'). But it declines gradually and ends humane, with the bakery men defending him and the request for flowers on Algernon's grave: nearer the loneliness dock of The Martian 82 than 1984 60, about 1 to 3 points.

axis:momentum.note: Mild. The misspelt first tens of pages slow a recurring minority ('Ten začátek se mi tak špatně četl, že jsem myslela, že to snad ani nedočtu'; one reader set it down near page 70 and came back), and the arc is visible early. Many others read it in a sitting. A point or two, the drive complaint of Počítání hvězd 85 rather than a stall.

axis:density.note: The novel expands the 1959 story, and the commonest Czech complaint is a padded middle: 'kniha je o 100 stran delší než by měla být', 've střední pasáži jsem se chvílemi trochu nudila', the reason given being 'milostné tokání'; a Goodreads 3.5 says the middle 'started to feel like dragging'. The padding sits mostly in the romance thread, while the same expansion carries the childhood memories that earn on the protagonist axis. A point or two.

axis:character-differentiation.note: Each wants something different: Rose a normal son, Fay the moment, Alice the man he was before the change, and Norma, who resented him, reconciles late. A minority call the women types ('The Cruel Mother, The Whore, and The Angel'), against Budrys's praise for its 'rounded characters'.

axis:faith.note: A minor thread taken seriously, never mocked: a nurse says the scientists tamper with 'God's plan', a woman likens his new knowledge to the sin of Adam and Eve, and Rose took him to church. No satire of religion.

axis:sex-portrayal.note: No one-sided contrast: the scientists he overtakes and the bakery men who mock him are men, and Alice, Fay, Rose and Norma are not written as cleverer than anyone.

axis:unearned-competence.note: The genius is given by surgery, but the gift is the premise under examination rather than an authorial convenience: it costs him his friends and Alice, and a rule he discovers takes it back.

axis:life-phase.note: Charlie is 32 throughout. The childlike voice of the first and last reports is the disability shown from inside, and the childhood scenes are an adult recovering memories, so this is not the Ender's Game 87 case of a child's inner life.

axis:multi-pov.note: One first-person diary from start to finish.

axis:memoir-form.note: A fictional diary whose form is the premise (spelling and register rise and fall with his IQ), not testimony, so the diary failure of The Diary of a Young Girl 40 does not transfer.

axis:short-idea-driven.note: This is the full novel, not the 1959 story, so the short-form suspension neither applies nor is needed: ideas, motives and lead earn on their own.

axis:childrens.note: An adult novel; it is read in schools, but the novel 'goes more into depth of the adult themes' than the story.

axis:content.note: Rose's beatings, bullying and workplace cruelty are shown seriously and serve the story; violence and swearing are not objections.

axis:sequels.note: Standalone novel; no sequel or prerequisite.

axis:opening.note: Read from the Albatros ukázka (Pátková translation, pp. 7-19). A boy bursts into Koreander's antikvariát to escape bullies. In dialogue we learn he is 'deset jedenáct let', was held back a year, his mother is dead and his father 'nikdy nic neříká'. He steals the book, locks himself in the school attic and opens it. That is one thread with full context before Fantastica appears. Chapter II (also sampled) states outright what the Childlike Empress is before Cairon names Atreyu.

axis:occult.note: No rite is staged. Wishing through AURYN is the only magic: a badge of the Empress's commission, with no invocation, devotion or priesthood. The sorceress Xayide steers hollow armour by will. The German character article finds no ritual scenes or spell rites; the only ritual mentioned is Atreyu's hunter initiation, interrupted. A flag for the reader, not a deduction: the motto 'Tu was du willst' and the 'true will' theme match Crowley's Thelema. Ende said he took the motto from Rabelais and Augustine, and religious critics (Klaus Berger) read the book as occult.

axis:detective.note: Atreyu's Great Quest seeks a cure for the Empress through the Southern Oracle and the Old Man of Wandering Mountain. It has no crime, clues or culprit, and the second half has no investigation strand.

axis:worldbuilding.note: Declared rules are kept. The Empress lives by names. The Nothing spreads because humans stopped coming. A Fantastican swallowed by it becomes a lie in the human world (Gmork). Bastian has 'nur noch so viele Wünsche wie Erinnerungen', and the count runs to the last. The cross-world question the rule asks, who crossed and stayed, is answered in the City of Old Emperors. Minority dissent: 'proč se svět Fantazie rozpadá jen proto, že císařovna nemá jméno?' (databazeknih, 2 stars). The name rule is declared rather than explained, and the rules oblige no explanation.

axis:protagonist.note: Bastian is a lead with real flaws to overcome (coward, liar, thief). The ending goes the way the rule rewards: he sees the Old Emperors he would become, is 'consumed by shame', wishes to love, and back home confesses the theft. But the vain, Xayide-led stretch, which ends in war at the Ivory Tower and wounding Atreyu, is staged on the page, not uncovered from a past. It is the most named complaint: 'Bastien je pěknej zmetek', 'Bastiena jsem od poloviny knihy zuřivě nesnášel'. About -4 to -6.

axis:motives.note: Chapter II's interlude puts Bastian's grief on the page: the surgeon's 'upřímnou soustrast', a father behind an 'neviditelná zeď'. The second half peels back his wants one by one (beauty, strength, admiration, wisdom, belonging, to be loved, to love), each priced by a memory. Fantasy Book Review dissents: the Atreyu friendship is asserted, and Ende 'doesn't show any actual evidence of it'.

axis:ideas.note: The Gmork scene is named 'Nejsilnějším momentem Nekonečného příběhu' and read as Orwellian by Czech reviewers. The motto is turned into a search for one's true will and resolved in the wish to love: 'imagination is only useful when constrained by sufficient wisdom'. The ideas are treated seriously inside the world's rules. Dissent: 'overwhelming preachy tone' (Goodreads), 'příliš výchovná' (databazeknih), and a 'philosophical inconsistency' between the halves (Fantasy Book Review).

axis:density.note: Critics agree on the second half: 'rinse and repeat', 'Just one damned thing after another', 'Postavy se objevujou a mizí'. Several name the refrain 'ale to je jiný příběh' as an irritant. Every episode spends a memory on one arc, and Nikolajeva notes the halves mirror each other. So this is The Lord of the Rings 84's thin-for-its-length cost, not Unfinished Tales 69's fragmenting. About -3 to -4.

axis:momentum.note: The first half is fast, and the midpoint is where readers stop: 'A po půlce jsem odložila', 'Dcera vydržela knížku číst do poloviny', 'Od té části, kdy je Bastián povolán do Fantázie... rozhodla knihu odložit', and 'will this ever end?' on Goodreads. This is the problem named in Pocitani hvezd 85. About -2, kept small because it overlaps density.

axis:childrens.note: Albatros sells it 'Věk od 10'. Adult critics split: 'Hlubší, temnější a dospělejší' and 'far more interesting for adults', against 'určena spíše pro čtenáře ve věku kolem deseti let' and 'všechno se tam děje hrozně jednoduše a lehce'. The adult layer is real. About -1 to -2.

axis:life-phase.note: Bastian is 'starý tak deset jedenáct let' and Atreyu is a boy too. Bastian's inner life is a child's: crying, fear of school, hunger in the attic. That is the Ender's Game 87 shape. About -1 to -2.

axis:bleakness.note: Reader content warnings list animal death (Artax in the Swamps of Sadness), death of a parent, violence and war. None of it is sustained, and the book ends in reconciliation with the father.

axis:faith.note: No religion is played for satire. The Water of Life reads as rebirth, a 'secularized baptism'. Berger attacked it as a counterfeit of salvation, and Prondczynsky saw 'christologischem Mystizismus'. Either way the register is serious.

axis:prophecy.note: Uyulála's answer is that only a human child can name the Empress. The Old Man writes all that happens, and the story loops until Bastian acts. Foreknowledge never bends for the plot. Bastian's self-made saviour role ('vystupující jako spasitel celé Fantázie') is shown as hubris, earnestly rather than cynically.

axis:unearned-competence.note: Bastian's wished strength and beauty are handed to him, but that is the subject and it is priced: memory loss, and Nikolajeva's 'false hero'. A reader puts it as 'pseudo-hrdina ktorý je vo všetkých kategóriach najlepší, až na jednu, na ustráženie svojho ega'. The dull invincibility is counted under density.

axis:multi-pov.note: Two strands are printed in two colours, Bastian's attic and Fantastica. The Fantastica side is a staggered relay (messengers, then Cairon, then Atreyu), traced by one databazeknih reviewer.

axis:sequels.note: A standalone novel; the films are separate works.

axis:sexual-content.note: The plot is the Nothing, the quest and Bastian's wishes. Nothing in it is about sex.

axis:sexual-treatment.note: It is published as a 10+ children's book. A reader's content warnings list animal death, body shaming, death of a parent, violence and war, and nothing sexual. A few StoryGraph reviewers tag 'sexual harassment' as moderate, with no referent found; the bullying is the likeliest.

axis:infidelity.note: Bastian's mother is dead and his father widowed. There is no marriage strand.

axis:same-sex-romance.note: No romance for either lead. The plot summaries show none.

axis:sex-portrayal.note: There is no competence contrast. The wise and powerful are mixed: the Empress, Uyulála, Morla, Dame Aiuóla and Xayide, beside Cairon, Graograman and the Old Man. Reactor's critic calls Ende's gender views conventional, 'rather tedious', which is the opposite direction from this axis.

axis:verse.note: Uyulála speaks only in rhyme for one episode. The book is prose.

readingOrder: standalone: first novel of its lead (Úžasná Zeměplocha 30 in the Czech numbering), no earlier volume needed

axis:opening.note: The screening's 'page one' claim is wrong by a few pages: two short prologues (sunken ships watched by an unexplained golem; a young clacksman on a new tower whose line is cut) precede chapter one and mean nothing until later. Chapter one itself, read in full in the publisher's excerpt, is a single thread with context supplied as it goes ('Lord Vetinari, under whose idiosyncratically despotic rule Ankh-Morpork had become the city where... everyone wanted to live'), so neither filter shape fires; a Czech reader: 'Máloktorá pratchettovka ma chytí od prvej strany, ale tejto sa to podarilo'.

axis:occult.note: Small graded deduction, a point or two. Golems are animated by 'holy words' (chem) placed in their heads by priests, the Discworld form of the golem legend; here that is lore at one remove (Anghammarad 'baked by the priests of Upsa', Moist guessing at 'a scroll, or something') and no making is shown, while on the page golems are run as robots under an amended First Law. No rite is staged elsewhere: the haunting letters, the space-bending sorting engine and the wizards' omniscope involve none, and Moist's temple prayers are a con, priced under faith.

axis:detective.note: Not investigation-shaped. The villain is shown to the reader early (Horsefry blurts 'There is no proof that we had anything to do with the boy's murder!' to Vetinari), the dead postmasters are a few chapters of Moist asking questions that the haunted building answers itself, and the fraud is exposed by a con (a forged clacks message 'from the dead'), not by detection.

axis:worldbuilding.note: The clacks are a declared technology whose ownership drives the plot: taken from its inventor by financial trickery, run down by a chairman who 'knew full well his policies would drive the business into the ground', answered by stamps, golem postmen and a man-in-the-middle hack; a Czech reader: 'Celé to dávalo zmysel, nebolo to veľmi absurdné'. Held below the top because comic devices run beside it (a pi=3 sorting engine, the omniscope), one reviewer notes Moist 'does benefit from quite a lot of luck' though not deus ex machina, and a 3-star reader found the loose ends 'protivné'.

axis:protagonist.note: Interior and flawed from page one ('what had he actually done that was bad, as such? He'd only been moving numbers around'), with the direction of travel the reader rewards: Mr Pump working out that his frauds have killed 2.338 people, then Moist recognising Adora's lost job as his own forgery scam and confessing; one review calls it 'one of the most convincing redemption stories I've ever read'. A minority dissents: 'neskutečně nesympatická postava... nefandíte mu' (3*), 'a standard-issue Picaresque', he 'never has to confront the darkness of his personality'.

axis:motives.note: Every principal wants something specific and the plot is those wants colliding: Moist to live, then to win, then to be unlike Gilt; Adora justice for her family; Gilt money through a con with vision; Groat a promotion; Pump his freedom. Critics find the cast 'černobílé' and short of 'emotional power', which caps this rather than reversing it.

axis:ideas.note: Freedom including 'the freedom to take the consequences' (Vetinari, chapter one), hope as the con man's product, public infrastructure stripped for profit, corporate doublespeak quoted at length by a Czech reviewer; another reads it as 'základní argumenty proti absolutní svobodě'. Against: 'too obvious, too straight-forwards and loud', 'moralizující', and one 5-star reader says there are 'žádné filosofické úvahy'.

axis:faith.note: With the Post Office burnt, Moist takes stamped letters to the gods round four temples, fakes a vision and digs up his own buried loot as a gift from the gods; the city then crowds the temples for windfalls, a lottery parody. Religion played for laughs, but the gods are the setting's invented odd-job pantheon and the target is the con and credulous hope rather than belief itself; one to three points.

axis:momentum.note: Chapter one is fast, then several readers stall: 'the first several hours were kind of boring', 'had to push myself to get to about the 150 page mark', 'Poté mi četba chvíli zadrhávala'; and several call the end rushed ('slabší konec', 'mrzí rychlý konec', 'The last 20% ... lost me a little'). Others report the opposite ('Napínavé od začátku do konce'), so a mild cost, a point or two.

axis:character-differentiation.note: A distinct cast each with its own logic (Groat and his remedies, Stanley and pins, Pump, 'Spike' Dearheart, the piratical Gilt, Vetinari, an ancient golem postman); Czech readers single out the 'řadu drobných rázovitých postaviček'.

axis:unearned-competence.note: Moist's skill is a con man's trade established in chapter one, and it fails him when it matters: he cannot see how to win the race and has to go to Adora honestly. One reviewer's 'rarely struggles' is the dissent.

axis:sex-portrayal.note: Cleverness is mixed: Moist, Gilt and Vetinari are the top operators, Adora is sharp and Groat proves valuable; Adora sees off a drunk by pinning his foot with a heel, the creative-not-strength case the reader credits.

axis:sexual-content.note: A courtship that ends in a kiss ('like kissing an ash tray, but in a good way'); no sex scene in any summary or trope list.

axis:sexual-treatment.note: Innuendo at the level of a joke about the tallest building on the top-value stamp ('How like a man'); nothing crude.

axis:same-sex-romance.note: The romances are Moist and Adora and an elderly pair reunited by a forty-year-late letter; none same-sex.

axis:infidelity.note: The reunited couple are 'both elderly and widowed'; no marriage is betrayed.

axis:multi-pov.note: Chapter one holds Moist alone; cutaways (Vetinari's meeting with the Grand Trunk board, a girl in a clacks tower) arrive later, one at a time.

axis:density.note: Complaints are about pace, not padding; 521 pages in Czech, 'těch 500 stránek knihy téměř zmizí před očima'.

axis:life-phase.note: An adult lead, 'about twenty, or about thirty' by the narrator's own account.

axis:sequels.note: Not a continuation: a new lead and institution introduced from scratch, read as an entry point ('pro nováčky skvělý vstupní bod'; an English reviewer new to the series found it worked standalone). Recurring city figures appear at cameo level.

axis:opening.note: Read in the Czech publisher's excerpt (Host 2021, pages 9 to 38, the opening story): one narrator addressing the caliph gives his name, city, trade and grief on the first page ("v srdci jsem měl soužení") and walks into one shop. The three nested tales then arrive one at a time, each announced and closed before the next. The Czech order matches the English, per the track list of the Czech audiobook (Host and Audioteka) and Legie.

axis:collection.note: The front is the strongest part of this book, the reverse of Já, robot 55: the opening story is the piece Czech readers most often name as best ("to je nejlepší povídka sbírky", "Lepší úvod som dlho nezažil"), the title story splits them (a favourite for some, "vůbec nebavila" for others), and the third runs seven minutes of the Czech audiobook, too short to stall anyone. The exposure is the fourth story, priced under axis:density.

axis:ideas.note: Every early story has a one-sentence idea: the past cannot be changed, only understood, ending on "Můžeme se kát, můžeme vše odčinit a může nám být odpuštěno. To je vše, avšak to stačí"; life runs on a pressure difference that is running out; a device proves the future fixed. Fate and belief are taken seriously inside the story's own rule, the handling praised in Světlo věcí konečných 96. Later pieces carry personhood, memory against truth, and choice across branching worlds.

axis:worldbuilding.note: The title story declares one mechanism (thought is air moving gold leaf) and follows it to every consequence, the clocks seeming fast because brains slow and then the end of the world, read in the publisher's own released text. The gate story states its rule early ("Komnata zůstává stejná bez ohledu na to, kterými dveřmi vejdete") and every tale closes its loop under it, where the Three Laws broke in Já, robot 55. One soft spot: the very short third story asserts rather than argues that a one-second precognitive light drives people into akinetic mutism, a leap a commenter on the Nature page contests.

axis:protagonist.note: The opening story's narrator confesses that he parted from his wife with words he is ashamed to repeat, after she objected to his slave-trading, freed the slaves he had bought, and has spent twenty years praying, fasting, giving alms and repenting: a man facing his past and refusing to be it, the direction-of-travel clause. The title story's narrator is a curious anatomist who dissects his own brain to learn the truth. The cost sits in the fourth story, where a critic finds Ana's and Derek's inner lives "more than a little simplistic" and told rather than shown.

axis:motives.note: The gate story and its nested tales are each about what one person wants (a fortune, a stolen fortune, a younger husband, forgiveness), with almost no action. The digient novella is a decade of argument over what caretakers and digients should want, and the closing novella is, in a critic's words, about "flawed characters making bad decisions and trying to make better ones".

axis:occult.note: The gate is offered as a mechanism and explicitly not sorcery ("Jsou to čáry?" "Ne, pane. Nikdy jsem se nesetkal s džinem... Toto je jistá forma alchymie"), explained as a widened pore in reality like a worm's tunnel and made in a workshop of copper coils and mirrors, which is how its power is conferred, with no invocation. Astrology and geomancy are only mentioned, and a street astrologer's offer is turned down with a laugh. The prayers in the first and eighth stories are to God in a sincere religious frame, which is faith and is priced under axis:faith, not a rite of an occult system.

axis:detective.note: No story is a mystery. Two investigation-shaped strands, both flagged: the title story's narrator asks why the clocks run fast, a scientific question rather than a crime, and the eighth story has a short strand in which the archaeologist follows clues to a relic thief and catches her.

axis:density.note: The digient novella runs 3 h 16 min of the Czech audiobook's 11 h 19 min, close to 29% of the book, and is the commonest complaint: "zbytečně natažený", "desítky stran poměrně nezajímavým textem", "vyloženě nebavil a musel jsem se hodně nutit", and "meandering" in English. It has defenders too (one Czech reader reread it four times). About -2 to -4: a thin stretch in one long piece, not a thin book.

axis:momentum.note: Several pieces explain a concept more than they tell a story ("simply do nothing but explain the concept"; "někdy dokonce chybí samotný děj"), and two Czech readers say they had to force themselves through. A fresh premise every story restarts the drive, so this is the Počítání hvězd 85 shape: a point or two, not a stall.

axis:faith.note: The opening story is devout Islamic piety played straight ("Na počátku všech věcí stojí Alláh"), faith as a thread inside a story about fate, nothing mocked. The eighth story makes faith its subject, a devout scientist's prayers in a world where young-earth creation is proven, who learns humanity may not be the purpose of creation and returns to her work for its own sake; most critics read it as serious ("avoids both parody and credulity"), one as gentle satire, and three Czech readers balked at the creationist premise. About -1 to -3, late in the book, and not the Já, robot 55 failure.

axis:sexual-treatment.note: Low volume, no crudeness: the opening story's third tale has one non-explicit page in which a wife leads her husband's younger self to a darkened bedroom and teaches him "umění lásky", and the digient novella's second half turns on a sex-doll company's offer to train digients as companions, argued as a question of consent with no scene in any source. One chapter still cost Válka starého muže 87 a few points, so about -1.

axis:sexual-content.note: No story's plot is about sex. The sex-companion offer is one funding option in a novella about raising digital minds; remove it and the novella stands.

axis:infidelity.note: The opening story's third tale is titled "Příběh manželky a jejího milence" and tells a faithful wife's decision to "následovat hlas své touhy" with a young man who turns out to be her own husband before he has met her; she keeps it secret afterwards. With no third party neither the premise veto nor the subplot bands apply, but an approving frame on an apparent affair sits in the first story, and the fourth adds a married man's unacted attraction to a colleague. About -1.

axis:same-sex-romance.note: No plot summary of the nine stories carries a same-sex romance and no review or content list consulted mentions one; cleared at premise level, not checked line by line.

axis:short-idea-driven.note: The suspension covers the cast-less early pieces (the third story is a warning addressed to the reader), and each early idea is nameable in a sentence. It adds nothing on its own; the points are on axis:ideas.

axis:sex-portrayal.note: No one-sided contrast in the opening story: the wisest figure is the old alchemist, the morally clear-sighted ones are the wives (one opposes the slave trade, one demands the stolen money be repaid, one outwits the thieves), and the men are flawed but neither foolish nor diminished.

axis:bleakness.note: Three pieces face an ending (a universe running down, a world losing its will, a species going extinct), but each turns toward consolation: "Contemplate the marvel that is existence, and rejoice that you are able to do so", and the opening story ends on repentance and forgiveness. Elegy, not the misery of 1984 60.

axis:prophecy.note: Foreknowledge comes only through the gate and obeys its declared rule, that the future can be learned and never changed; the narrator's predictions to the caliph at the end are a future he has already lived. Nothing bends when the plot needs it.

axis:character-differentiation.note: The three nested tales give three distinct wants and ways of thinking: a trusting rope-maker, a weaver who robs his own future, a wife acting on her own desire.

axis:multi-pov.note: The nested tales arrive one at a time, each introduced and closed, and the closing novella alternates two viewpoints.

axis:life-phase.note: The leads are adults, most of them middle-aged or old; no early story is told from a child's inside.

axis:opening.note: Read from text: the first page (Albatros 2008, p. 7, quoted by bibliohelp) and the official Albatros sample for pp. 12-20, which covers chapter 2 and the start of chapter 3. There is one first-person voice and one situation: 'Budu vam povidat o svem bratrovi... Jonatan vedel, ze brzy umru.' Chapter 2 is the fire, told partly through a newspaper report, and chapter 3 opens 'Pak se to stalo' with Karl at the gate in Cherry Valley. Jonatan has described Nangijala before Karl arrives, so every invented name comes with its context. Neither shape of the filter applies, and one rater says: 'Po prvni kapitole mate pocit, ze je konec... Ale je. A jak!'

axis:occult.note: Checked against the whole system, including how power is conferred. The dead reach Nangijala, and those who die there reach Nangilima, only by dying (accident, illness, the final leap), never by a rite. No god, priest, prayer or invocation appears anywhere in the plot. Katla obeys whoever holds Tengil's horn because she fears its sound, which makes it a device, not a spell. Prisoners fed to her are executions, not offerings, and nobody worships her. The closest case is in chapter 2: a white dove at the window, in whose cooing Karl hears Jonatan's voice ('Zni to asi trochu strasidelne'). It comes unasked and Karl puts no question to it, the reverse of Havran 40, where the narrator interrogates the bird. That makes it a visitation, not divination.

axis:detective.note: There is a traitor strand: the doves carrying messages to the resistance are being shot, so someone in Cherry Valley is informing. Karl first suspects the wrong man (Hubert), then simply overhears Jossi meeting Tengil's soldiers. Nothing is worked out from clues, so this is a flag, not a deduction.

axis:worldbuilding.note: Little is declared, and what is declared is honoured. Karm, the serpent in the Karma Falls, is set up as a legend Katla hates and watches the water for before he appears. Losing the horn is what frees Katla. Katla's fire is what paralyses Jonatan, and the Nangilima rule is what the ending acts on. The author also refuses to rescue his leads: the horses, Hubert and Mattias die, and Jonatan is crippled. Adult readers poke at loose ends ('A cim vickrat umreme, do tim lepsiho sveta jdeme?'; how Jonatan knows of Nangijala at all). Nangijala is asserted in fairy-tale register, so the bar the author sets is low, as it was for Narnia 67. Lindgren privately accepted the reading that it is the dying Karl's fever dream.

axis:protagonist.note: Karl is ordinary, frightened and sure he is ugly, stupid and cowardly. His flaw is fear, and he overcomes it: he rides out alone, exposes Jossi, helps free Orvar and makes the final choice himself. A 5-star adult reread says 'neni to zadny typicky hrdina bez bazne a hany, ma strach, pochybuje o sobe, ale prave proto je jeho odvaha nakonec tak opravdova'. The cost sits in life-phase rather than here. Two adult raters marked it down for his endless self-belittling and crying ('mi sel vypravec na nervy, jak porad dokola omilal sve nedostatky'). Jonatan has no flaw to overcome; he is the co-lead, seen from outside through his brother's adoration.

axis:motives.note: The brothers want different things for different reasons. Karl wants safety and his brother. Jonatan goes into danger because 'annars ar man ingen manniska utan bara en liten lort'. Jossi sells out for Tengil's promise to make him ruler of Cherry Valley, a promise Tengil never meant to keep. The earn is modest: Tengil is evil with no account of why, which is the 1973 Goteborg critics' complaint that the book shows evil too schematically and never examines its roots.

axis:ideas.note: The idea can be named and is said on the page: courage is what you do while frightened. Around it are the fear of death, what may lie after it, and tyranny with resistance; one reader notes the compulsory rallies and a police state that can enter any home. Adult reviews keep returning to 'filozoficky presah' and compare it with The Little Prince 82 ('lze, podobne jako Maleho prince, ruzne interpretovat'). There is a dissent: 'Nemam pocit, ze by slo o ... knihu s filozofickym presahem vetsim, nez najdeme ve vetsine pohadek.' The contested part is the ending's message. Many readers call the leap 'navod na sebevrazdu'. Defenders, and the critics Matthias and Metcalf, read it as Karl overcoming his fear of a death already coming.

axis:short-idea-driven.note: It is short (152 pages in the 2024 Albatros edition, illustrated) and the idea can be named in a sentence, so the line's sparseness argument holds. But it is a continuous adventure narrative told from inside a child, closer to Narnia 67 than to an allegory like The Little Prince 82. The suspension of the character rules should not be assumed to waive the child-voice cost, and the rule adds no points.

axis:bleakness.note: Mild, about 2-4 points. The grief arrives at once, as in Promena 58: a dying child, his brother's death in chapter 2, 'by byvalo lepsi, kdybych misto nej umrel ja'. It lifts into an idyll by chapter 3, and the book is about companionship and self-sacrifice throughout ('Pribeh je plny nadeje, temnotu zde nehledejte'). The double death is the point of the book, not a twist. The adult objection to it is mostly moral rather than about mood: 'navod na sebevrazdu' appears in about six Czech comments, Goodreads has 'suicide is both acceptable and a not even all that traumatic escape', and The Horn Book in 1975 called it too shocking. No read book anchors that. It is priced at this rule's mild weight and sets the floor. The screening line's 'only 1984 60 ever triggered it' is out of date: Promena 58's bleakness risk fired too.

axis:childrens.note: Small, about 2-3 points. Albatros sells it for ages 9 and up and the prose is a child's. The adult layer is real (death, tyranny, courage), and adult raters split. Some say 'knizka, ktera da vic dospelym, nez detem' or 'nejlepe ji pochopi dospeli'. Others say 'v dospelosti je pro me zas pribeh az moc detsky' or 'asi nejsem ta spravna cilovka, nejspise uz jsem vyrostl'. That puts it between The Hobbit 84, which paid nothing, and Narnia 67, which paid.

axis:life-phase.note: A couple of points. Karl is ten and reads as ten from the inside. He cries a great deal and runs himself down, and he talks like a child ('Pani, jsem tak rad'). This is the Ender's Game 87 markdown, not the type of lead.

axis:faith.note: An afterlife with no god: no deity, church, prayer or judgement, and Lindgren is usually described as agnostic. Religion is not the subject and is not mocked, so neither costed dimension applies. The biblical echoes analysts list (Katla and Karm as the beasts of Revelation and Job, Jonatan's self-sacrifice, the paradise valley) are reverent, not satirical. One Czech reader did object to the ending as a Christian ('Komentuji to jako krestan, ktery ma nadeji na vecny zivot'). That is the moral objection priced under bleakness, not a faith cost under the rules.

axis:prophecy.note: There is no prophecy. The Christ resonance (Jonatan dies saving his brother, 'dokonaly jako Jezis (a take se obetuje)' in one review) is earned by the plot and played straight, so the reverence test passes.

axis:momentum.note: Most raters describe a pull: 'napinava jak ksandy', 'tezko ji odkladate na pozdeji', 'jednim dechem'. A minority dissent: 'na me v nekterych chvilich trochu zdlouhave'; 'Nudne a nezazivne'; 'pribeh o ohrozeni bajne zeme je tak placaty a nudny'. A Goodreads reviewer finds the end rushed.

axis:density.note: About 150 illustrated pages with no padding: 'prosty, cisty, bez odbocek, zajimavosti a postrannich zapletek'.

axis:character-differentiation.note: The two brothers think and want differently. The supporting cast (Sofia, Hubert, Mattias, Orvar, Jossi) is functional, and Tengil is a type.

axis:unearned-competence.note: Jonatan is brave, kind and beautiful from the first page, but he is the narrator's idol seen from outside, not the lead. Karl's courage is earned across the book. His sudden ability to swim in Nangijala is the afterlife healing his body, not a skill handed to him.

axis:sexual-content.note: A children's book for ages 9 and up with no romance anywhere in the plot summaries: brothers, a resistance and a tyrant.

axis:sexual-treatment.note: No sexual references. It is a 9+ children's book whose plot has no romance.

axis:infidelity.note: None. The father 'odjel na more a od te doby jsme o nem neslyseli', which is desertion before the story starts, not infidelity, and it is never revisited.

axis:same-sex-romance.note: No romance of any kind. The bond at the centre is between brothers.

axis:sex-portrayal.note: Competence is mixed. Sofia leads Cherry Valley's side of the resistance and Orvar leads Thorn Rose Valley's, and Jonatan, Hubert and Mattias are all capable. There is no contrast between the sexes.

axis:content.note: The violence is real but within limits: Katla kills rebels in the final battle, prisoners are worked to death and fed to her, and the horses die. One rater wanted the battle cut ('barvite popsano valceni a zabijeni'), which concerns children as readers, not an adult objection.

axis:sequels.note: A standalone novel in Jarka Vrbova's translation, Albatros 2024; the payload's translator field is empty.

readingOrder: volume 1 of the Silo trilogy: read first; its own arc closes, and the origin of the silos is left to a later volume

axis:opening.note: Chapter one is a single thread, "The children were playing while Holston climbed to his death", and within it the reader learns he is the former sheriff, that his wife was sent out three years ago, and that he is going out to die; 'cleaning' is only half-explained, but the situation reads. Neither shape of the filter fires. A minority of Czech readers felt lost early ("Čtenář vkročí do děje a je zmatený"), and they tie it to the lead changes, not to chapter one.

axis:occult.note: Secular post-apocalyptic SF. Power is conferred by office under the silo's succession rules, and by IT's monopoly on information, with no rite, magic or supernatural element in the plot summaries, and none raised in the Czech comment threads searched.

axis:detective.note: Part 3 is investigation-shaped: as sheriff, Juliette "obsesses over these two closed cases" (her lover's death and Holston's file), recovers deleted server data and comes to suspect the later suicides. Czech readers call stretches of it "politická detektivka" and "konspirační detektivka". It is one part of five, and its object is the state's lie rather than a whodunit, so it is a flagged strand worth about -1 to -3.

axis:worldbuilding.note: The society holds as a control system (birth lottery, the forbidden question, cleaning as deterrent, suits built to fail), and the book explains why cleaners clean: the visor shows a green world, a lie planted in Part 1 and traced to its program in Part 3, and even a 3-star reviewer calls the world "pretty well-thought-out". The physical side has gaps this volume never closes: no lift in a 144-level shaft (Holston only notes the stairwell "had not been built for such abuse"), mass-produced guns, decades-old bodies and soup in the dead silo; these are peripheral to the premise, about -1 to -3. The silos' origin is deferred, which the scope rule neither docks nor credits.

axis:protagonist.note: Three leads in sequence, each rootable and interior: Holston (grief, his wife's reason left open), the mayor (duty, a late love), then Juliette for three parts, "strong-willed and not necessarily diplomatic" and, by one Czech reader's account, rash in Part 4, so she has flaws to work against. Each handoff is set up a part ahead. A minority disliked losing leads early ("sotva jsem si zvykla na nějakou postavu, zabili ji"), and many say the book settles once Juliette takes over.

axis:motives.note: Parts 1 and 2 are mostly about what characters want and fear, and the excerpted Part 2 chapters are mainly interior reflection and dialogue. The antagonist's case is real enough that readers sided with him: "Vlastně jsem Bernarda chápal". Docked within the axis for the uprising, whose cause some found thin and whose fighting runs long ("urputná bitka"); Ian Sales calls the antagonist "a pantomime villain".

axis:momentum.note: The most common complaint, from fans as well as critics: a strong Part 1, then a sag through the mayor's descent and the sheriff chapters to around page 200 ("2 old people climb stairs for 100 pages"; "První třetina knihy se neskutečně vleče"), then a gripping second half ("po půli se děj krásně rozjel"). Priced together with density at about -2 to -4, on the Počítání hvězd 85 anchor.

axis:density.note: Padding is the other half of the same sag: stair-walking and technical description ("snad čtvrtina knihy je jen o tom, jak někdo jde po schodech"), and Ian Sales calls the prose "very baggy". It is priced inside the momentum figure, not added to it.

axis:ideas.note: Truth against safety, and whether lying and killing keep a closed society alive ("úvah nad nutností lhát či zabíjet za účelem přežití"). Readers report changing sides ("mnohokrát váhala, na čí straně jsem"). A few critics found no deeper idea.

axis:bleakness.note: There are deaths and two suicides in the first half, but the ending is hopeful, to one reader "Až příliš happy end", and another notes the book lacks "tíživá, dusivá hrůza". Juliette's isolation in the dead silo ends when she finds a survivor and children, and her return to save Lukas is a self-sacrifice, so the 1984 60 shape does not apply.

axis:unearned-competence.note: Her mechanical skill is earned on the page, and she survives the cleaning because friends swap in good heat tape. Her later survivals strain readers ("nezničitelná super hrdinka", "Mary Sue hacker genius", "super-competent"), while others find her "celkem uvěřitelná": a mild dock, about -1 to -2.

axis:multi-pov.note: Parts 1 to 3 follow one lead at a time. Parts 4 and 5 alternate about three lines by chapter, each already anchored ("střídání úhlů pohledu v rychlém sledu udržuje čtenáře v napětí"). The threads are staggered, not simultaneous.

axis:character-differentiation.note: The cast is distinguished by role and by what each wants (sheriff, mayor, mechanic, IT head, the young stargazer, the old electrician); one reader: "Každá postava má svou vlastní hlavu". A recurring minority calls the cast black-and-white or flat; that complaint falls mainly on the antagonist and is priced under motives.

axis:sexual-content.note: Minimal: "several instances of kissing, and a mention of sex" (Rated Reads); "Referenced and a vague scene" (Elitist). Nothing close to the plot.

axis:sexual-treatment.note: No crude treatment is reported anywhere; the only sexual material is one reference and one vague scene.

axis:infidelity.note: No marital betrayal. The mayor's late love for her deputy comes decades after her husband's death, and the guilt in it is loyalty to the dead man, not an affair.

axis:same-sex-romance.note: Every romance in the plot (Holston and Allison, the mayor and her deputy, Juliette and Lukas) is heterosexual, and none of the content reviews mentions a same-sex relationship.

axis:sex-portrayal.note: Competence is mixed across the sexes. A man finds the illusion program and an old male electrician gets her the good tape, beside two capable women ("two strong female central characters"). The one gender note in the reviews runs the other way: husbands telling capable women to stay out of the fight.

axis:content.note: A war with "a fair amount of blood", and strong language "concentrated in about two or three places"; "brutal but not gory". Within the violence-and-swearing tolerance.

axis:opening.note: No excerpt could be loaded directly: the publisher's Everand preview is region-locked, and its first line ('To be the skipper of the only boat on the Moon was a distinction that Pat Harris enjoyed') is confirmed only through the search index. So this rests on readers independently describing the same opening: one tourist cruise across the Sea of Thirst with captain Pat Harris and stewardess Sue Wilkins, boat and dust explained before a moonquake swallows it ('Tady se jde přímo na věc. Šup lidi do plechovky. Bác.'), with the rescuers entering one at a time afterwards. Two Czech readers found the start slow ('přes těžkopádný začátek'), which is the legible-but-uneventful case the filter does not cover.

axis:occult.note: Nothing occult is staged. Radley's flying saucers, Atlantis and hidden 'others' are one passenger's conspiracy beliefs, mocked rather than enacted, and the astronauts' 'Outsiders' are a myth the book never makes real; the only antagonist is the Moon itself.

axis:detective.note: A passenger, Harding, stands up late to say he is a detective trailing Radley, an accountant who 'made off with stolen credit'. It is a single reveal among the trapped passengers, not a case the reader follows; the search for the buried boat is technical detection (an infrared heat trail seen from orbit), not a mystery.

axis:worldbuilding.note: The dust is declared once (bone-dry, flowing like a liquid) and every crisis follows from it: heat cannot escape through the dust and kills the air purifier, the passengers' waste turns dust to mud and causes a second cave-in, dust in the double hull shorts the batteries and starts a fire. Readers: Clarke 'follows all his conclusions through logically' (Goodreads), the setbacks 'never seem contrived' (infinity plus), 'byl tak přesvědčivý, že jsem mu věřil i ten nebezpečný (a neexistující) prach' (databazeknih). The period tech (printouts, photographs searched with a magnifier) irked a couple of Czech readers but is consistent with the level the book presents.

axis:protagonist.note: Pat Harris is rootable and not one-note: 'dependable, trustworthy and likable but is not the know-it-all hero' (SFFWorld), with 'a nagging doubt that he handed over authority, and relinquished power too easily' to the retired commodore Hansteen (astrofella), and he nearly wrecks the air line while drunk on CO2. But it is an ensemble with Hansteen out-leading him, and even fans call the cast thin: 'fairly lightly sketched' (Jo Walton), 'papundeklové obrysy s neuměle domalovanými xichty' (databazeknih). A few points under a Weir lead; the one-note lead of Artemis 69 is not what the evidence shows.

axis:motives.note: Does not earn, which the screening assumed it would. The drama is the rescue; the passengers' reasons surface in a mock trial and two late reveals, and Czech readers note that Clarke 'každou potenciálně zajímavou mezilidskou situaci rychle vyřeší, a jede se dál' and wanted 'větší důraz na psychologii pasažérů'. The page time goes on problem-solving, not set-piece action, so no deduction either: The Martian 82's balance.

axis:momentum.note: The consensus is a page-turner: 'as suspenseful a novel as I think Clarke ever wrote' (Black Gate), 'The tension never lets up' (Jo Walton), each fix followed by a fresh setback and a last-minute escape. The dissent is real and specific: 'bogs down into a bunch of people with slide rules digging a hole' (Goodreads), 'Dvě třetiny knihy docela nuda' (databazeknih), and authorial foreshadowing that cbdb readers say drains the suspense.

axis:sex-portrayal.note: The reader's stated objection, men written dumb against clever women, does not occur; the reverse does. 'The main characters are all men' (Jo Walton), women 'there to look pretty, become hysterical, or, ultimately, get pregnant' (infinity plus), and one Goodreads reader stopped at 50% because 'Women were all stewardesses, former burlesque dancers, or bitter virginal old maids'. Sue Wilkins is capable in her job. Priced at the mild dock, since this direction has no read anchor.

axis:sexual-content.note: The plot is the rescue; the Pat-Sue romance is one thread and ends in marriage in the epilogue.

axis:sexual-treatment.note: One love scene between Pat and Sue, 'tactfully veiled' (Goodreads; Black Gate has them 'embrace, privately'), plus a racy novel read aloud and passengers stripping down in the heat. Low volume and not crude, the Red Rising 95 position; one Czech reader recalls selling it to a classmate as 'mírně lechtivý' and being told it was a book for children. A sneer at a spinster's 'impacted virginity' is counted under sex-portrayal.

axis:faith.note: No religion is satirised. The mockery falls on Radley's UFO conspiracy-mongering ('sounds, alas, exactly like those today', Black Gate), which one Czech reader disliked as a sneer at believers in alien life; a passenger who refuses an injection on 'religious reasons' is hiding a drug history, a lie exposed rather than faith mocked.

axis:multi-pov.note: The boat, Lawrence's rescue, Lawson's search and Spenser's broadcast alternate after the sinking rather than starting together; 'svěží bylo i střídání děje v kabině a mimo ni' (databazeknih).

axis:density.note: Under 300 pages and praised for not being stretched. The one strand readers call filler is the journalist Spenser's, 'docela zbytečné odstavce... v závěru knihy zcela opuštěna' (databazeknih), and a couple found the engineering detail tiring; neither is the padding that cost The Martian 82 its ending.

axis:bleakness.note: Not bleak: a group facing it together, kept going by games and readings, and rescued, which is the companionship the reader preferred in Project Hail Mary 92 over the solitude docked in The Martian 82.

axis:character-differentiation.note: Passengers are told apart by their secrets (Hansteen's alias, Radley's saucers, Harding's badge, a physicist, a lawyer and his ex-dancer wife), though two Czech readers complain that the engineer Lawrence and the astronomer Lawson are too easily confused.

axis:opening.note: Read from the licensed preview: the narrative opens on one concrete scene with its context in place, the four friends lying in a field 'on the day we're the last people to see indie kid Finn alive', talking about love, before a boy runs past chased by a glowing girl. The italic header above it names an invented herald and a 'permanent Vessel' with no context, by design, and the narrator frames that as someone else's story at once ('They better not blow up the high school again'). Readers who stalled early, one DNF at about 50 pages, blame the frame's disconnect and slowness, not an illegible first scene.

axis:occult.note: The source test passes: the pantheon is invented (Jared's grandmother was a goddess of cats; there is a deer god), not a real-world tradition. The only rite is the villains' possession ceremony that puts their Empress into Satchel's body, and it exists only in the chapter-18 header summary of the off-stage plot, never dramatised; on the page there are cats coming to Jared 'for blessing', which he calls 'giving them benedictions', played as a running joke, and a bargain with the gods that widens his healing, reported in dialogue rather than staged. Nothing vetoes; one to three points, a judgement at the boundary rather than a measured cost.

axis:detective.note: No investigation strand: the deaths and disappearances belong to the off-stage plot, and Mikey's suspicion of the newcomer Nathan is one he admits to Jared is mostly jealousy.

axis:worldbuilding.note: The town is declared loosely: every few years the indie kids fight undead, soul-eating ghosts or vampires, the school is blown up and rebuilt, and most adults look away; the characters only theorise why, and the mother's politics are tied to her remembering the ghosts, so a consequence is carried and no mechanism is undertaken that could break. The one precise declaration, Jared's healing, is honoured: set up inside the first fifty pages ('one quarter God'), limited (it cannot reach mental illness), failing on a mangled mountain lion, and when a late bargain widens it the offer is made and refused on the page, so the screening claim of a capability declared and then dropped does not hold. The thin spot is how little the town reacts, which one reader notes leaves the big events unexplained.

axis:protagonist.note: Mikey is anxious, jealous and self-doubting, with a condition to work against: a reviewer with OCD calls it 'one of the first times I've seen symptoms similar to mine', down to skin that reddens and cracks, and the therapy chapter is the scene reviewers single out. His direction of travel is towards help, back to the therapist and medication. Dissent: two Czech readers find the cast shallow or 'na zabiti', with Jared the exception.

axis:motives.note: Page time is almost entirely what the four want and fear: Mikey's unspoken love for Henna and fear of losing his friends at graduation, Mel's recovery, Henna's refusal of her parents' mission trip, Jared's secret and the choice he makes for his friend; Reactor calls it 'pretty much' slice-of-life. One dent: Disability in KidLit finds Mikey's final refusal of the healing does not ring true.

axis:ideas.note: A nameable idea, that an ordinary life is not a lesser one, carried with a serious account of mental illness ('Anxiety is a feeling grown too large'; medication 'not a sign of defeat'). It is partly undercut at the end, where the ordinary kids' contribution runs through Jared accepting godhood: reviewers call it the 'only misstep' and say Ness 'kind of cheats', and Czech readers wanted 'vetsi presah'.

axis:momentum.note: The commonest complaint: 'Pretty much nothing happens' (a D-minus review), 'really boring' (the top Goodreads review), the frame 'acts like an anchor that drags the main plot's pace to a crawl', and on databazeknih about ten readers report slowness, one forcing through the first 100 pages and two stopping near page 50. Praise exists ('remarkably restrained pace', read in one sitting) and the book is short; two to four points, the shape Pocitani hvezd 85 carried.

axis:prophecy.note: No prophecy or fate theme: the chosen-one strand is genre parody in mock-epic headers, aimed at the would-be heroes' 'grandiose self-centredness', not at fate or belief. Most reviewers read it as affectionate ('isn't an attack on stories about Chosen Ones in the slightest'), a minority as 'snide' ridicule, and the ending plays Jared's godhood straight, as a sacrifice for a friend. Zero to two points.

axis:same-sex-romance.note: Below premise: Jared, the best friend and one of the four leads, has been secretly seeing Nathan, revealed after prom with a real falling-out between him and Mikey, and the two end together. Mikey himself 'messed around' with Jared in the past, says he is not gay, and 'casually wonders at a couple of points if he might be partly gay'. Lighter than a protagonist's own ongoing relationship but a recurring thread rather than background: three to six points, a magnitude the log cannot measure separately.

axis:sexual-content.note: Not the plot: one encounter between Mikey and Henna with 'little description other than the sentence, We slept together', after which they settle as friends; the book is about graduation, family and friendship.

axis:sexual-treatment.note: Low volume and low explicitness ('no graphic details'), but teenage-boy frankness: the first kiss described with his erection, masturbation mentioned, a lost virginity, and, per one content review only, a past encounter with a 27-year-old waitress who gave him crabs. The crudeness is light but present, and Valka stareho muze 87 shows a little still registers; two to four points.

axis:life-phase.note: High-school seniors whose inner life is prom, a crush, finals and graduation, written as a teenager from inside; a point or two for a reader of 28.

axis:childrens.note: YA (rated 14+) in an adult-readable register, with alcoholism, therapy, frank sex talk and swearing; the register of The Hunger Games 89, not a children's book.

axis:multi-pov.note: One first-person narrator; the second line is a single italic paragraph per chapter, staggered, never a simultaneous fan-out.

axis:character-differentiation.note: Each of the four has distinct wants and troubles (Mikey's OCD, Mel's eating-disorder recovery, Henna's missionary parents, Jared's divine heritage and secret); called 'credible, kind-hearted' by Reactor and distinct by a Czech reader, while dissenters find them flat.

axis:bleakness.note: Heavy material (OCD, an eating disorder, an alcoholic father, suicidal thoughts raised in therapy) handled warmly and with humour; Common Sense rates the positive messages 'a lot' and the ending is hopeful.

axis:faith.note: Henna's devout missionary parents are a character thread, and she declines their trip at 18; the narrator jokes about churches and his politician mother does not believe in evolution 'at least politically', which satirises a politician, not belief. Not religion played as satire.

axis:content.note: Strong language 'used sparingly', teen drinking after prom, and violence that 'mostly happens around the main cast'; within the tolerance.

axis:unearned-competence.note: Jared's power is inherited but bounded (it fails on a mountain lion), and widening it costs him his future as a god after college; the effortlessly gifted indie kids are the parody's target and stay off-stage.

axis:sex-portrayal.note: No reviewer reports a one-sided contrast; competence is mixed across the sexes (Jared heals, Mel and Henna act for themselves, Mikey carries his younger sister out of the concert bombing).

axis:infidelity.note: No affair: the father's duplicity is money taken from his brother-in-law, and the romances are between unmarried teenagers.

axis:opening.note: Small, 1-3 points; neither shape of the filter fires. An authorized anthology reprint of chapter one (Gunn, 1979) shows one thread, a parade and keystone ceremony and then a dinner at which Estraven withdraws his support, with the stakes stated at once ('I was in peril of my life, and did not know it'), the mission named ('to bring about an alliance between Gethen and the Ekumen') and most terms glossed as they arrive ('the kyorremy, the upper chamber or parliament', 'shifgrethor - prestige, face, place, the pride-relationship'); the political subtext stays opaque, but the narrator says so himself ('understand nothing except the animosity between Tibe and Estraven'). The cost is term density and a slow start, then a jump to a folk tale in chapter two: 'prvni pulka zmet nevysvetlenych pojmu' and 'rozjezd me temer odradil' (cbdb), 'Dost dlouho mi trvalo, ze jsem se zorientovala v deji' (databazeknih), a Goodreads reader 'looking for a glossary of terms'.

axis:occult.note: Moderate, five points off both ends. The Handdara Foretelling in chapter five is a working rite staged once on the page with the narrator in the circle: he pays the Fastness, nine Foretellers (the Weaver, Celibates with one in kemmer, a Pervert, two Zanies) sit in the dark, he is drawn into their 'web', and the Weaver, seen as 'a woman dressed in light', screams 'Yes!', which comes true; critics call it 'the ritual practice of the foretelling'. It does not fail Source: the Handdara is invented and godless, with no deity, clergy or borrowed real-world practice, and its only likeness to real divination is the shape of asking seers a question; Genly frames it as hunch trained 'to run in harness', 'not so much a prophecy as an observation', and the faculty as extrasensory ('not a specific aspect of that religion', LitCharts), so the rule's own moderate case, an invented religion's foretelling answered, fits, while the lack of any technical account keeps the mechanism escape out of reach. Nothing else raises it to heavy: the Yomesh founding vision and a chapter-four tale of a lord asking the day of his death are lore, the chapter-one keystone set in blood mortar is a civic ceremony using animal blood ('We use the blood of animals, these days') with human sacrifice only as a past custom, and mindspeech and dothe are declared faculties.

axis:detective.note: No investigation. The first half's question is why Estraven withdrew his support and what he wants, answered through his own journal chapters and the trek rather than worked out from clues; the second half is an escape from a labour camp and a crossing of the ice.

axis:worldbuilding.note: The declared biology (latent most of the month, then kemmer in either sex) is carried into the society: no war in its history, any adult may bear a child (the king becomes pregnant mid-novel), shifgrethor governs politics and the cold shapes everything; 'Svet je vybudovany naprosto mistrovsky, veril jsem tomu' (cbdb), 'svet je to detailne propracovany' (databazeknih). The dissent is the premise face: critics from Lem on say the Gethenians read as men, Czech readers say the androgyny 'na pribeh jako takovy nemela prilis velky vliv' and is 'povrchove pozlatko', and Le Guin herself conceded the pronoun and the heterosexual default. The declared consequences are carried and the gap is presentational, so it trims the credit rather than costing.

axis:protagonist.note: Genly has flaws to overcome and a direction of travel: distrustful, reading Estraven's manner as 'this soft supple femininity that I disliked and distrusted in him', and he unlearns it on the ice; a Czech reader says his misogyny gives him 'osobni dimenzi', and Estraven, exiled for doing right and spending himself to save him, is read as 'the true hero'. The dissent is coolness rather than flatness: 'ani Genly Aie, ani Estravena jsem si vubec nedokazal oblibit' (cbdb), side characters 'kartonove' (databazeknih), events 'brushed off too quickly' by the stoic narration (Goodreads).

axis:motives.note: Page time goes to what people want rather than what they do: the first half turns on misread motive (why Estraven withdraws, why the Orgota welcome the envoy), Estraven's journal chapters answer it, and the trek is two people learning what the other wants; 'clovek v hroznem osameni hleda a mozna najde spojence na zivot a na smrt' (databazeknih). Readers note how little happens ('Absence deje, pribehu, zapletky', cbdb), the shape that tops the log in Speaker for the Dead 90.

axis:ideas.note: Nameable in a sentence: what is left of politics, loyalty and love when sex is taken out of them, set against patriotism as fear of the other ('Znamena to nenavidet svou nezem?') and a religion that foretells only 'to exhibit the perfect uselessness of knowing the answer to the wrong question'. Readers praise exactly this ('Hlavni cil - primet ctenare, at premysli o urcitych tematech - se podle me povedl na vybornou', databazeknih; 'mam na chvilku o cem premyslet', cbdb); the dissent is that the gender theme reads as agenda ('prvoplanovy aktivismus... narazky na gender, genderovou teorii a sexualni mensiny', cbdb) or 'didn't lead anywhere' (Goodreads).

axis:momentum.note: Moderate, three to six points. The first half is political and slow ('the plot was terribly slow for the first half', Goodreads; 'Prvni polovina bylo vylozene utrpeni', cbdb, rated 20%; 'pomerne hodne hlucha mista, ktera se dost nudne tahnou', databazeknih; one Goodreads DNF at page 180), and nearly everyone says it takes off with the escape: 'posledni tretinu jsem jiz hltala', 'od urcite casti uz to jelo svizne'. Pocitani hvezd 85 shows weak drive costing points without leaving the S band.

axis:density.note: 230 Czech pages (Argo), so length cannot pad it; the complaints of little plot ('Absence deje, pribehu, zapletky') and long landscape and weather passages ('nudne popisky krajin a pocasi', both cbdb) are the slow first half, priced once under momentum.

axis:bleakness.note: Small, 0-2 points.
